html:
A dialogue on the best form of state, written by Cicero in six books between 54 and 51 BCE, as the Roman Republic slid towards civil war.

It is modelled on Plato's Republic but is about Rome. Cicero sets it in 129 BCE in the garden of Scipio Aemilianus, who leads the talk. The best state, Scipio argues, mixes the three simple forms: kingship, rule by the best, and rule by the people. Rome, with its consuls, Senate and assemblies, had such a mix. The idea goes back to the Greek historian Polybius, a friend of the real Scipio.

The work ends with the Dream of Scipio, in which Scipio's dead grandfather Scipio Africanus shows him the heavens and the smallness of earthly fame. That part survived through a commentary by the late Roman writer Macrobius and was much read in the Middle Ages.

Most of the rest was lost. In 1819 the scholar Angelo Mai found large pieces in the Vatican Library, under a later text by Augustine written over the scraped parchment.
sum: A dialogue on the best form of state, written by Cicero in six books between 54 and 51 BCE, as the Roman Republic slid towards civil war.
